
{{< include ../_includes/_lab-helpers.qmd >}}

::: {.todaymeta}
Four parts, on the Europeanisation and the economy case study
:::

:::: {.todaybox}
::: {.nonincremental .fs-70}
1. The claim and credibility – the credibility debate, the three Rs, the SCORE robustness study, and the paper with its record in SCORE
2. The estimand and the causal graph – what a claim asks, and what a graph commits you to
3. The reproduction – one of three recorded results, three models and few clusters
4. Robustness – the menu, the class chart, the curve, a replication and the declared analysis
:::
::::

::: {.todaytake .fs-80}
You leave with a reproduced result, an estimand and a causal graph, and two dots on the class chart
:::

::: {.todaymeta .fs-80}
Work in the IDE workspace, in Positron, RStudio, VS Code or another IDE; these slides show every step
:::

::: notes
Welcome. We spend the day on one published claim, in the four parts listed on the slide. The first asks why the credibility of social science is argued about, what 'replication' names and what the SCORE robustness study did, and it ends on the paper, with what SCORE found when it tried to reproduce and to replicate it. The second asks what quantity the claim is about and what a causal graph commits you to. In the third you reproduce one of three recorded results, and the three models behind them lead to the problem of few clusters. The fourth takes the analysis apart decision by decision, reads the multiverse on the class chart, and ends on the one analysis that you declare before you run it. You work in your IDE workspace throughout, and these slides show every step with its output.
:::

## Two kinds of aim {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**What I want you to understand**

- Why 'replication' names three operations, and what each one tests
- What an estimand is, and why analysts who disagree are often answering different questions
- What a causal graph commits you to, and what fixed effects and random intercepts each adjust for
- Why 27 countries are few clusters, and what the CR2 test does about it
- What a specification curve establishes, why hundreds of estimates are not hundreds of tests, and what preregistration settles
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**What I want you to be able to do**

- Reproduce a recorded result to the third decimal
- Write an estimand in one sentence, and a graph whose adjustment set you derived
- Read fixed-effects and random-intercept models of the same claim side by side
- Vary one decision at a time and say what changed and why
- Preregister one analysis before you run it, and place it among the alternatives
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
The left-hand column holds what I want you to understand, and today it is the more demanding of the two: the estimand, the causal graph, what fixed effects and random intercepts each do to a comparison, why twenty-seven countries make few clusters, and what a set of results can and cannot establish together. Each aim on the right ties those ideas to something that you do yourself, a reproduction, a graph, three models read side by side, a round of exploration and a preregistration.
:::

# PART 1 – The claim and credibility {#part-1-the-claim-and-credibility .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 1
:::

::: notes
Part 1 begins with why the credibility of social science is argued about, including the red-card study, in which twenty-nine teams analysed one dataset and reached different answers. The grid of the glossary then separates reproducing from replicating, and the SCORE robustness study shows how five analysts reanalysed the claim on which we work today. After the paper itself and its record in SCORE, we open the IDE workspace and these slides, so that everybody is running before the break.
:::

# PART 2 – The estimand and the causal graph {#part-2-the-estimand-and-the-causal-graph .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 2
:::

::: notes
Part 2 carries the main argument of the workshop, that analysts who seem to disagree are often answering different questions. We follow Lundberg and colleagues in their three steps from a theoretical estimand to an empirical one and then to estimation, and we go through causal graphs in full, with confounders, mediators, colliders, paths and what fixed effects adjust for. The part ends on our own claim, on your estimand in one sentence and on the half-built graph that you finish in the hands-on.
:::

# PART 3 – The reproduction {#part-3-the-reproduction .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 3
:::

::: notes
Part 3 is the reproduction, to the third decimal, of one of three recorded results. The three models reproduced by the class are three estimators, so we read them side by side, and then ask what conventional errors hide when twenty-seven countries carry all the evidence. We end on what a reproduction needs besides the data and the code, on the slips carried by the pipelines of the analysts, and, if time allows, on reading the code deposited by your analyst.
:::

# PART 4 – Robustness {#part-4-robustness .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 4
:::

::: notes
Part 4 is robustness. We go through the menu decision by decision, from the outcome scale and its construction, claim alignment, the predictor and its form and what fixed effects absorb, to the copredictor, the sample and the weights. You then work the menu yourself and send the analysis that you would defend to the class chart. We read what the class built against the five analysts, ask which decision moves the estimate most and why hundreds of estimates on one dataset are not hundreds of tests, and take up what a replication of this claim would have to fix in advance. The part ends on the critics, on what preregistration settles and on the one analysis that you preregister before it runs.
:::
